comment: Every `#[cfg(not(unix))]` behaviour arm in rust/crates/*/src, with the verdict a reviewer gave it. scripts/ci/platform_arm_inventory.py keeps this list honest.

arms.note: Windows normalises the path lexically. `GetFinalPathNameByHandle` is not ported, so a junction or a symlink component is not followed to its target and a path that aliases into a trusted root still reads as being inside it.

Opens the cache root by path instead of holding a directory handle for `openat`. The root is under the account's own private state directory, so no second account can swap a component between the probe and the read.
Reads a pinned object by path with an existence probe instead of `fstatat` against a held handle. Same reasoning as `new`.
Publishes with write-then-rename instead of `linkat` from an unlinked temporary. Rename is atomic on NTFS; the only loss is a stray temporary file after a crash, not a torn object.
No mode-bit probe, so the resolved Git path always reads as executable. The caller still requires it to canonicalise onto the host's own Git executable, which is the load-bearing half of that check.

`st_dev`, `st_ino` and `st_mode` have no stable Windows reading, so identity falls back to size and mtime. The tuple is used to notice a file that changed under the scan, not to prove two paths are the same file.
`launch_identity` is replaced by `launch_identity_stub.rs`. Wrapper-resolution launch identity is POSIX-only, so Windows callers require re-approval instead of reusing a saved one.

The POSIX `launch_identity` module is stubbed off Unix, so the same hash material is built inline here. The two have to stay in step: a field added to `package_request_launch_identity_material` has to be added here as well.
No reusable launch command off Unix, so approval reuse lands on `launch_identity_unstable` and asks again. Conservative, and one reason Windows prompts more than macOS for package work.

PATH resolution on Windows admits any existing file; executability there is an ACL and `PATHEXT` property, not a mode bit. `PATHEXT` is not applied, so a candidate without an executable extension can still be picked.
Same reading as `mcp_decision::is_executable_file`: an existing regular file is the Windows answer for an executable PATH candidate.
Returns false, so no Bun preload candidate is admitted as an executable file and the command stays reviewed. Fails closed.
Launcher shapes are recognised only on Unix, so a chain that would be allowed there stays reviewed on Windows.
No private scratch parent off Unix: `%TEMP%` ownership is not probed, so a temporary target is never admitted and the write stays reviewed.
A contained publish never recognises its check launcher off Unix, so the command stays reviewed.

One of the two arms this inventory was written for. `cd`-containment callers have no execution sink on Windows, so a sibling repository root is never resolved and a command that would run contained there is reviewed instead. PR #5200 shipped this stub with a `#![cfg(unix)]` integration test, so nothing ever exercised it. Closing it needs a Windows containment sink, not a different return value here.
Windows takes its own `#[cfg(windows)]` arm in this file; this one covers platforms Guard does not ship for.

Without the restricted launchers every setting counts as forwarded, so an environment-prefixed command is never admitted as plain data and stays reviewed. Fails closed, as the comment on the arm says.
A Git hook is executable on Windows by being a file Git will run, not by a mode bit, so every regular file in the hook directory is treated as live. Stricter than the Unix arm, not weaker.
An inert hook directory is never recognised off Unix, so `git init` chains that reuse one stay reviewed.
Every regular file counts as executable, because Windows has no mode bits to read. Stricter than the Unix arm: more probe targets are treated as runnable.

The shared roots this guards are the POSIX ones (`/tmp`, `/var/tmp`). Windows gives each account its own `%TEMP%`, so no caller passes a root that this could police, and the Unix ownership walk has nothing to answer for.
A repository owned outside home is never recognised off Unix, so the route stays reviewed.
A `--git-dir` route is never admitted as in-scope off Unix, so it stays reviewed.
Sticky shared roots are a POSIX concept and are never recognised, so a temporary Git route stays reviewed.
Ownership below a shared root is never proven off Unix, so the route stays reviewed.

The hard-link count is skipped, so a file with a second link into it is still read. `number_of_links` needs a by-handle query that `std::os::windows::fs::MetadataExt` does not expose on stable, so closing this needs a `GetFileInformationByHandle` call. The caller still bounds the file by size and requires it to be a regular file.

The group- and other-writable mode check is skipped, so a kubeconfig in a directory that other accounts can write is still trusted. The surrounding checks still require the file to sit outside the agent's own trees and outside any repository. Closing it needs an ACL read, not a mode mask.

arms.item: fn resolved( model: &CanonicalCommandV1, reason: &'static str, cwd: Option<PathBuf>, context: PathContext<'_>, ) -> Option<&'static str>
arms.note: Only the Node build and Node tool reasons are filtered here; every other contained reason is passed through for `generic.rs::windows_contained` to decide. That allowlist is where a Windows containment profile is actually admitted.
Resolves the staged tool entry by name the same way the Unix arm does; the entry names are platform-neutral.
Probes the installed `node_modules` tree by path. pnpm markers are rejected the same way; the only Unix-specific part (`symlink_metadata` on a linked package) reads reparse points on Windows.
The socket-directory ownership walk is POSIX-only, so a local Postgres probe is trusted without it. Windows clients reach a local server over TCP loopback, where there is no socket directory to own.
Windows takes its own `#[cfg(windows)]` arm in this file; this one covers platforms Guard does not ship for.
Windows takes its own `#[cfg(windows)]` arm in this file; this one covers platforms Guard does not ship for.

In-place `sed` editing of an executable file is reviewed on Unix by its mode bits. Windows carries executability on the extension instead, so this arm reads the extension against `EXECUTABLE_EXTENSIONS` and reviews a `.ps1`, `.bat`, `.cmd`, `.exe` or other runnable target the same way.

The extensions Windows runs directly, standing in for the Unix mode bits. `.js` is in the default `PATHEXT` and is left out on purpose: it is ordinary repository source far more often than a script. Compiled into test builds on every platform so `windows_executability_is_read_off_the_extension` covers it.
Case-insensitive extension lookup behind the non-Unix `executable`. Compiled into test builds everywhere, so the Unix suite proves it too.
A loader directory under home is never trusted off Unix, so the command stays reviewed.

`!agent_writable_loader_tree` reads true off Unix, so a loader directory the agent can write is not excluded on that ground. The condition it sits in still requires the directory to be trusted some other way, and `home_loader_directory` above it is false on Windows, so the disjunct it belongs to cannot admit a home directory on its own.

No workspace sandbox on Windows, so no workspace is admissible and every command that would run contained is reviewed. This is the gap behind the Windows false positives; see docs/guard/windows-platform-coverage.md.
The Linux namespace sandbox does not exist off Unix. Paired with `workspace_admissible` above.

arms.item: pub(super) fn outside( _model: &CanonicalCommandV1, _workspace: &Path, _context: PathContext<'_>, _execution_environment: Option<&GuardExecutionEnvironmentV1>, ) -> bool
arms.note: Workspace containment is not admitted off Unix, so the launch-outside-roots probe has nothing to answer and returns false.
Workspace containment is not admitted off Unix, as the comment on the arm says.
The exact workspace shape is recognised only where the restricted launchers exist, so the settings route stays reviewed.

Checks only that the leaf is not a symlink. The Unix arm walks the chain of parents with a hop bound, so an aliasing component above the destination is not caught here. Junctions report as symlinks to `file_type`, so the leaf check does hold for them.
Check-then-open instead of `O_NOFOLLOW`: the metadata probe rejects a reparse point and the open follows. A swap between the two is a narrow race inside a directory the account owns.
Device and inode are unavailable, so sameness is decided by canonicalising both paths and comparing them case-insensitively, which is how Windows itself compares paths.
No `O_NOFOLLOW`, so a reparse point left on the runtime path is followed. The path is under the account's own installation directory.
The uid ownership walk up to the root is skipped. The caller still requires the candidate to sit under the private root it was given. Closing it needs an ACL owner read.

arms.item: pub(crate) fn private_directory_owned_by_current_user( _: &PyPath, _: u32, _: Option<&fs::Metadata>, ) -> bool
arms.note: A private owner-only directory is never proven off Unix, so the body-file read is refused. Fails closed.
An existing regular file is the Windows reading of an executable; mode bits do not exist there.
Uses the read-only attribute as the writability signal. ACL-denied writes are not seen, so a directory can read as writable and the write then fails on its own.
Without POSIX file identity the config read cannot be verified, so it fails closed with an I/O error after the same path validation the Unix arm does.
An existing regular file is the Windows reading of an executable; mode bits do not exist there.
There is no root-owned notion to probe, so a system-owned wrapper is never recognised as trusted and the command stays reviewed.
Depends on `path_is_root_owned`, which is false off Unix, so no symlink component is ever trusted.

Uses the read-only attribute instead of the write mode bits. An ACL that denies writes is not seen, which makes the arm permissive in that narrow case, but it is paired with `path_is_root_owned` above, which is false off Unix and already refuses.
Returns the Windows file-attribute mask where the Unix arm returns a POSIX mode. Callers must not read permission bits out of it; they use it for the file-type and reparse-point flags.

`os.access(R_OK|X_OK, effective_ids=True)` has no Windows equivalent, so the directory reads as readable and a real read failure surfaces later as an I/O error instead of as an unreadable working directory.
The eaccess probe returns true off Unix. Paired with `directory_is_readable` above.
Refuses a symlink, junction or any other reparse point component before creating or writing, which is the Windows spelling of `O_NOFOLLOW` on each component.
There are no process groups, so only the direct child is killed and its own children can outlive it. A Job Object is the Windows mechanism for this and is not used here.
Windows has no termination signals, so an exit code is the whole answer; `-1` stands for a status with no code.
`os.access(X_OK)` has no Windows meaning, so every path reads as executable. Callers pair it with an existence and non-directory check.
There are no mode bits to add, so this succeeds without doing anything.
The executable bit is dropped because Windows has no such bit; a created file carries the inherited ACL of its parent. The parent is still resolved through the bound directory handle.
Entry names are not resolved off Unix, so AIBOM path scanning yields nothing there.
`~user` has no Windows meaning; only the current account's `~` is expanded.
Every AIBOM skills entry point returns `native_runner_authority_aibom_skills_unsupported` off Unix.
Opens the transition lock through the Windows private-root path; the file is still required to be under the account's private state root.
Takes the advisory `fs2` exclusive lock and validates the opened file, as the Unix arm does; only the POSIX-specific identity checks are absent.
There is no parent-process reparent check to make, so `original_parent` is zero and the inspection is bounded by the caller's own budget.

arms.item: fn run_inspection( _request: &ArchiveInspectionRequestV1, _caps: ArchiveCaps, _original_parent: i32, _started: Instant, ) -> ArchiveOutcome
arms.note: Archive inspection does not run off Unix; the outcome names the unsupported platform.
Synthesises the conventional POSIX mode for the staged entry because Windows metadata carries none. The value is written into the containment manifest, not used to make a trust decision.
Probes reachability by opening the path (or reading the directory) instead of calling `access`, which is the reliable Windows answer.
Spawns the fallback and returns its exit code because Windows has no `exec`. The shim stays resident as the parent for the child's lifetime.

arms.item: pub(crate) fn exchange( _socket: &Path, _trusted: impl Fn(&Path) -> bool, _messages: &[Value], _deadline: Instant, ) -> Result<Option<Map<String, Value>>, Failure>
arms.note: The Codex app-server exchange runs over an AF_UNIX socket; off Unix the exchange is unavailable.
Ingress is not recorded off Unix because the contained bridge does not run there.
Validates the state path and derives the Guard home from it by path, which needs nothing POSIX-specific.
Absoluteness is decided by `Path::is_absolute`, which reads drive-qualified Windows paths correctly.
No contained workspace is resolved off Unix, so the Codex bridge does not route a command into a sink.
No snapshot is written off Unix; paired with `resolved_workspace` above.
The Codex version probe does not run off Unix, so updated input is never assumed to be applied. Fails closed.
`~user` has no Windows meaning; only the current account's home is resolved.
A trusted owner-only Unix socket has no Windows equivalent here, so no socket is trusted.

arms.item: fn attachment_reader( &self, attachment_root: &str, relative: &[String], max_bytes: u64, ) -> Option<Box<dyn std::io::Read + '_>>
arms.note: Without `openat` the walk cannot be descriptor-relative, so the path is resolved once and required to stay under the resolved attachment root, with the same `.`/`..`/empty rejections.
The daemon's command line is not read off Unix, so the pid is not matched against a trusted `ps` path.
There is no uid, so the host reports none and callers that compare ownership skip that comparison.
No executable file is recognised off Unix, so the direct tool context stays unresolved.
The account's home is not read from the password database off Unix, so Git's global-config checks have no account home to bound.
`getgroups` has no safe binding off Unix, so group membership is unknown and group-writable path checks cannot be satisfied.
Windows treats every existing path as executable because mode bits carry no ACL evidence, as the comment above the arm says.
The Git binary path is never proven trusted off Unix, so a Git execution that depends on that proof stays reviewed.
Global config environment stability is never proven off Unix.
A global push hook is never trusted off Unix.
Every existing file reads as an executable PATH candidate; Windows carries executability in the ACL and `PATHEXT`, not in mode bits.
Device and inode are unavailable, so workflow-file identity falls back to size and mtime. It is used to notice a file that changed between two reads.
Ownership is not proven off Unix, so nothing is treated as owned by the current account. Fails closed.
There is no POSIX file key off Unix, so the write cache never claims a cached identity and re-reads instead.
`~user` has no Windows meaning; only the current account's home is resolved.

The other arm this inventory was written for. Every contained hook route defers with `ContainedRouteFailed` off Unix, so a command that would run contained on macOS is reviewed on Windows. PR #5397 shipped this with `#![cfg(unix)]` test files, so the Windows arm never entered a test binary. Closing it needs a Windows containment sink.
There are no POSIX permissions on the store to repair.
Decodes the environment block from UTF-16, which is what Windows gives; the Unix arm decodes bytes.
There is no private mode to set on a path; the file is created under the account's own private state root, which carries the ACL.
There is no private mode to set on a handle; same reasoning as `set_private_mode`.
There are no process groups, so only the direct child is killed. Its own children can outlive it; a Job Object is the Windows mechanism and is not used here.
There is no POSIX file key off Unix, so the read cache never claims a cached identity and re-reads instead.
A root-owned, restricted managed-policy path is never proven off Unix, so managed policy from such a path is not trusted.
Creates the directory without POSIX mode bits; the restriction comes from the inherited ACL of the managed-policy root.
Creates the file exclusively and writes it; the restriction comes from the inherited ACL rather than from a mode.
Administrator context is not detected off Unix, so managed policy never takes the administrator path.
Holds the lease by file handle; the Unix arm additionally pins the owner directory, which Windows does not need because the handle itself blocks deletion.
Holds a plain `File` where the Unix arm holds an owner-marker lock, and keeps no directory lock. The exclusive handle is the Windows equivalent.
Unlocks the held file on drop; there is no directory lock to release.
Windows takes its own `#[cfg(windows)]` arm in this file; this one covers platforms Guard does not ship for.

Returns true because Windows residents use an authenticated loopback endpoint instead of a filesystem socket. The authenticated stopped acknowledgement and the owner-lock probe in the caller are the listener-containment checks there, as the comment on the arm says.
There is no filesystem endpoint to remove; the loopback endpoint is torn down with the listener.
No `SIGKILL`, so the child is killed with `TerminateProcess` and its descendants are not reaped. A Job Object would close this.
No `SIGKILL` for the supervisor either; same reasoning as `terminate_managed_child`.

arms.item: pub(super) fn serve_unix_managed( _owner: (&Path, &super::ManagedOwnerLock), _policy_store: std::sync::Arc<crate::policy_store::PolicySnapshotStore>, _generation: u64, _owner_process_id: u32, _digest: &str, _token: [u8; crate::AUTH_TOKEN_BYTES],
arms.note: There is no AF_UNIX managed listener off Unix; Windows serves the authenticated loopback transport instead.
There are no termination signals, so the exit code is the whole status.
There is no execute bit to restore on the bundled runtime.
Paths are UTF-16 on Windows, so the bytes come from a lossy UTF-8 encoding of the path rather than from the raw `OsStr` bytes.
The reason code the non-Unix `build` returns; paired with the arm below.
The native path model is POSIX, so a Windows host fails closed with `native_package_context_build_unsupported_platform` rather than guessing at Windows path semantics.
`~user` has no Windows meaning; only the current account's home is resolved.
Opens the snapshot read-only without the POSIX open flags; the file is under the account's own private state root.
The POSIX errno set that `pathlib` reads as a false predicate has no mapping here, so no error is ignorable and the caller surfaces it.
There is no owner uid to compare, so a request that carries one is refused and one that does not is admitted. Refusing the mismatched case is the conservative half.

arms.item: fn connect_unix_with_digest( endpoint: &str, timeout: Duration, identity: &ExpectedProcessIdentity<'_>, ) -> Result<BoxedResidentStream, String>
arms.note: There is no AF_UNIX client off Unix; the Windows resident is reached over the authenticated loopback transport instead.
Every contained execution operation returns `native_operation_unavailable_on_this_platform`. This is the resident-side face of the containment gap.
Windows takes its own `#[cfg(windows)]` arm in this file; this one covers platforms Guard does not ship for.
Validates the state document without the POSIX endpoint scope check; the Windows transport is validated by the branch below instead.
Rejects a state document whose transport is not the expected one, which is where the Windows loopback endpoint is checked.
Opens the state file read-only without the POSIX open flags; it is under the account's own private state root.
Publishes state with no Unix endpoint identity, because the Windows transport carries its identity in the authenticated loopback handshake.
There is no AF_UNIX listener off Unix; `serve_loopback` below is the Windows transport.

Only `contained_argv`, `normalized_command` and the Windows inline and Node-build planners answer off Unix. There is no pytest backend, which is why `source .venv/bin/activate && pytest -q` cannot be routed into a sink on Windows.
There is no uid, so the host reports none and ownership comparisons are skipped.
Durable business-budget accounting needs POSIX directory syncing, so it is refused off Unix with `native_business_budget_durability_unavailable`.
Directories cannot be fsynced off Unix, so the claim index commits without the directory barrier the Unix arm takes.
There are no termination signals, so the exit code is the whole status; `-1` stands for a status with no code.
The pre-commit hook is not installed off Unix because the hook directory cannot be proven to be a real trusted directory there.
Paired with `install_precommit_hook`: uninstall refuses for the same reason.
Paths are UTF-16 on Windows, so bytes from Git are decoded lossily instead of being taken as raw `OsStr` bytes.
`OsString::from_vec` is Unix-only, so a staged path is decoded lossily; a non-UTF-8 staged path on Windows still resolves through Git's own argv decoding, as the comment above the arm says.

arms.item: fn run_git_blob( root: &Path, args: &[std::ffi::OsString], ) -> Result<crate::git_read::CompletedOutput, crate::git_read::GitError>
arms.note: Runs Git with string arguments instead of `OsString` ones, for the same reason as `staged_blob_args`.
Device and inode are unavailable, so file identity leaves them unset.
Mode and link count are unavailable, so identity leaves them zero. Windows identity is carried by the file-id read the caller does separately.
Compares length and mtime where the Unix arm compares device, inode, link count and write mode. The caller pairs this with a `GetFileInformationByHandle` file-id check on Windows.
There is no ctime to compare, so the identity comparison above is the whole answer; the caller's Windows file-id check covers the rest.
